Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Ruby/gem process downloading payload from git.disroot.org (SleeperGem) AIDelivery High
Hunts the SleeperGem dropper stage where a Ruby interpreter (triggered by require-ing git_credential_manager) fetches a shell script and native binary from the attacker-controlled Forgejo instance git.disroot.org/git-ecosystem with TLS verification disabled. The download host + Ruby initiating process is the highest-fidelity single IOC in the campaign. Rationale: Anchors on the exact download host git.disroot.org (verbatim code block 3) paired with a Ruby-family initiating process, which is the dropper's Net::HTTP fetch (VERIFY_NONE). git.disroot.org is a legit privacy-community Forgejo instance, so the Ruby process filter removes benign user traffic. Cross-checked against The Hacker News and SC Media coverage confirming the git-ecosystem repo path. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/sleepergem-uses-three-malicious.html • https://www.scworld.com/brief/sleepergem-attack-targets-ruby-ecosystem-with-malicious-gems
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately browsing a real project mirrored on git.disroot.org via a Ruby-based CLI (rare)
  • Internal tooling that scrapes public Forgejo instances for OSINT
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating the sample in a lab that reports back to prod EDR
  • A gem legitimately named similarly that hosts assets on Disroot (none known)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("lab-detonation","sandbox") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the InitiatingProcessCommandLine shows a require/gem-load context and pull the resolved IP + any child powershell/sh process on the same host within 60s. 2) Contain: isolate the developer endpoint, block git.disroot.org at the proxy/DNS, and quarantine ~/.gem and the project's vendor/bundle path. 3) Hunt: enumerate Gemfile.lock across the fleet for git_credential_manager, Dendreo, fastlane-plugin-run_tests_firebase_testlab; pivot on any host that resolved git.disroot.org in the last 30d.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "git.disroot.org"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby.exe","ruby","gem","bundle","bundler","rake","irb")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "git.disroot.org"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ruby interpreter spawning PowerShell -ExecutionPolicy bypass or /bin/sh (SleeperGem dropper) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the SleeperGem execution stage where the gem's load-path hook hands the downloaded payload to a shell: 'powershell -ExecutionPolicy bypass "<path>"' on Windows or '/bin/sh "<path>"' on Unix, spawned by a Ruby-family parent. The ruby.exe -> powershell + ExecutionPolicy bypass parent/child pair is rare in normal developer activity. Rationale: Directly encodes the two verbatim Process.spawn strings from article v2.8.0: 'powershell -ExecutionPolicy bypass "..."' and '/bin/sh "..."' with a Ruby-family parent. The ExecutionPolicy-bypass branch is high-fidelity on Windows; the Unix-shell branch is kept for coverage (hence hunting tier). Sentinel query is Windows-only as SecurityEvent 4688 carries no Unix shell telemetry (noted). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/sleepergem-uses-three-malicious.html
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ruby build tooling (rake/bundler) legitimately shelling out to sh for native-extension compilation
  • Ruby-based deployment scripts invoking powershell for Windows provisioning
  • IDE/test-runner plugins that wrap PowerShell with -ExecutionPolicy bypass
  • chef/puppet Ruby agents spawning shells for configuration management
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("rake","spec","rspec") and FileName in~ ("sh","bash") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("make","gcc","cc","configure"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for a path under a temp/gem-cache dir and confirm the parent ruby was loading git_credential_manager (check same-host network hit to git.disroot.org). 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, and remove the dropped script + any native binary named after the masqueraded tool. 3) Hunt: on Unix, check for new cron entries and systemd unit files written within minutes of the shell exec; on Windows, look for scheduled tasks / Run keys created by the same session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby.exe","ruby","gem","bundle","bundler","rake","irb")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","zsh")
| where (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "ExecutionPolicy" and ProcessCommandLine has "bypass")
      or FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\ruby.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\gem" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\bundle.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\rake"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has "ExecutionPolicy" and CommandLine has "bypass"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 3d4e5f60-7a8b-4c1d-9e2f-0a1b2c3d4e51

SleeperGem malicious gem artifacts written to gems path (git_credential_manager / Dendreo / fastlane-plugin) AIDelivery High
Hunts installation of the three SleeperGem-compromised gems by watching for their package names written under a RubyGems gems/specifications directory. Catches both direct install of git_credential_manager and transitive pull-in via the trojanised Dendreo dependency. Rationale: Uses the three exact gem names named in the article/second sources. Requiring a gems/ or specifications/ path element removes coincidental filename collisions (e.g. a source repo literally called git_credential_manager) and keys on the RubyGems install layout. Dendreo is anchored with the '-<version>' gem-directory pattern to avoid matching the company name in unrelated docs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/sleepergem-uses-three-malicious.html • https://www.scworld.com/brief/sleepergem-attack-targets-ruby-ecosystem-with-malicious-gems
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A team that legitimately used the real (pre-compromise) Dendreo gem pinned to a clean version
  • Mirror/offline gem cache syncs that pull the full index including these names
  • Security tooling that stages the malicious samples for analysis
  • A developer cloning the legit git-credential-manager project (dash-form, not underscore) — excluded by underscore match
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("defender","mssense.exe") or FolderPath has "MpEnginedb")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the gem's .gemspec / lib load hook to confirm the git.disroot.org fetch and the CI-skip check, and identify the installed version (2.8.0-2.8.3 for git_credential_manager). 2) Contain: gem uninstall the three packages fleet-wide, pin known-good versions, and rotate any credentials (esp. git credential helpers) touched on affected laptops. 3) Hunt: correlate install time with subsequent git.disroot.org network hits and ruby->shell spawns; audit Gemfile.lock in CI/repos for the malicious dependency edge from Dendreo.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has "gems" or FolderPath has "specifications")
| where FolderPath has_any ("git_credential_manager","fastlane-plugin-run_tests_firebase_testlab") or FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)[\\/]Dendreo-\d"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFilePath has "gems" or TargetFilePath has "specifications")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("git_credential_manager","fastlane-plugin-run_tests_firebase_testlab") or TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)[\\/]Dendreo-\d"

SleeperGem Unix persistence: cron/systemd/LaunchAgent write by Ruby-descended shell AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the SleeperGem post-exploitation stage on developer laptops where the native daemon establishes persistence via cron jobs and systemd services (and LaunchAgents/Daemons on macOS), written by a Ruby-family or shell process. Corroborated by The Hacker News reporting of cron+systemd persistence after CI-evasion. Rationale: Targets the cron+systemd (and macOS Launch) persistence that second-source reporting (The Hacker News) attributes to the SleeperGem native daemon, scoped to a Ruby/shell writer to reflect the gem->/bin/sh->daemon chain. High FP by nature (config-management tooling writes these paths), so shipped as hunting with a Ruby/shell ancestry constraint. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/sleepergem-uses-three-malicious.html
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1543.002 T1543.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible/Chef/Puppet/Salt agents (often Ruby) writing systemd units and cron entries
  • Developer install scripts (curl|sh) that register a systemd service or LaunchAgent
  • Homebrew/rbenv post-install hooks creating LaunchAgents on macOS
  • Package managers writing cron.d entries during legitimate app installs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","chef-client","puppet","salt-minion","cloud-init","rbenv","homebrew"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written unit/cron/plist and check whether it launches a binary named after a common tool from a user-writable path or references git.disroot.org; correlate the writer process back to a ruby require. 2) Contain: disable+remove the persistence artifact, kill the daemon, isolate the host, and rotate developer credentials/SSH/git tokens. 3) Hunt: sweep for the native binary drop (same name as the masqueraded gem tool), other hosts with the same unit/cron name, and any beaconing to git.disroot.org or its resolved IPs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/systemd/system/","/lib/systemd/system/","/etc/cron.d/","/var/spool/cron/","/etc/crontab","/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby","sh","bash","dash","zsh","gem","bundle")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("ruby","gem","bundle")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/systemd/system/","/lib/systemd/system/","/etc/cron.d/","/var/spool/cron/","/etc/crontab","/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ruby","sh","bash","dash","zsh","gem","bundle")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WordPress wp2shell batch REST API pre-auth RCE exploitation (CVE-2026-63030/60137) AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP requests to the WordPress core REST batch endpoint /wp-json/batch/v1 (or rest_route=/batch/v1) that carry the batch-route-confusion + author_exclude/author__not_in SQL injection used by the wp2shell pre-auth RCE. Article-specific: anchors on the exact entry-point path plus the injected SQLi parameter and time-based payload tokens. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim article/PoC strings: entry path /wp-json/batch/v1 and rest_route=/batch/v1 (Code Block 1/2) plus the SQLi injection parameter author_exclude/author__not_in and time-based SLEEP() payload confirmed by the Searchlight write-up and the public detection PoC. Endpoint + non-GET method + SQLi token is very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://github.com/Senanfurkan/wordpress-cve-2026-63030 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-wp2shell-wordpress-core-flaw-lets.html • https://securityonline.info/wordpress-pre-auth-rce-cve-2026-63030/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate first-party plugins/mobile apps that batch REST calls through /wp-json/batch/v1 (no SQLi tokens present, so the SQLi selection filters them)
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Nuclei/Nessus/wp2shell.com checker) probing the batch route from known scanner IPs
  • Security researchers or the site owner testing exposure with the published PoC
  • WAF/CDN health checks that touch REST routes but not the batch endpoint with injection params
Suppression filter
| where not (src IN ("10.0.0.0/8") AND like(user_agent,"%HealthCheck%"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests to /batch/v1 from the source IP over the prior 24h; check scStatus (200 with post-shaped response body indicates the route-confusion succeeded) and confirm the target WordPress version is < 6.9.5 / < 7.0.2. 2) Contain: block /wp-json/batch/v1 and rest_route=/batch/v1 at the WAF/CDN, force the site to 7.0.2 (or 6.9.5), and rotate DB credentials if injection returned data. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same host — look for web-daemon-spawned shells and newly written .php files under wp-content/ within minutes of the request.

Web server daemon (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp) spawning a shell or network tool — wp2shell post-exploit code execution AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation stage of the wp2shell RCE: a WordPress web worker (php-fpm, apache2/httpd, nginx, or IIS w3wp/php-cgi) spawning an interactive shell or egress tool (sh/bash, nc/ncat, curl/wget, python/perl, cmd/powershell). Article-specific because the flaw yields arbitrary code execution under the web user with no plugin involved. Rationale: Article states the flaw 'chains into remote code execution' against a stock install under the web user; the highest-fidelity host signal for that is a WordPress web daemon (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp) parenting a shell or egress binary — a parent+child pairing that is abnormal for a web server. Parent set is WordPress-specific, not a generic LOLBin template. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-wp2shell-wordpress-core-flaw-lets.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress plugins that legitimately call exec()/shell_exec() (e.g. image optimizers invoking convert, backup plugins invoking mysqldump/tar)
  • WP-Cron or deploy hooks running via php-fpm that shell out to curl/wget for remote fetches
  • Server management panels (Plesk/cPanel) whose PHP workers spawn shells for admin tasks
  • CI/CD or WP-CLI automation executed under the web account during scheduled maintenance
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp","-i","bash -c","sh -c","-e /bin","base64 -d","|sh","| sh","IEX","-nop")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for reverse-shell/download syntax (/dev/tcp, nc -e, bash -i, curl|sh) and correlate the timestamp against UC1 batch-endpoint hits on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending php-fpm/worker child tree, and pull the box out of the load balancer. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by that PID (UC3) and outbound connections from the web daemon; capture bash history and /tmp for staged payloads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","netcat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentProc=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProc=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","nc","ncat","netcat","curl","wget","python","perl","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New PHP file written into WordPress web root by a web daemon — wp2shell web shell drop AIInstallation Medium
Hunts web shell persistence following the wp2shell RCE: a WordPress web worker (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp/php-cgi) creating a new .php/.phtml/.php5/.phar file under wp-content, wp-admin, or wp-includes. Article-specific because unauthenticated RCE in core is routinely followed by dropping an attacker PHP payload into the web-accessible tree. Rationale: WordPress web daemons should not author new PHP files in the web root outside of an update; pairing the web-worker writer (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp) with a fresh .php under wp-content/wp-admin/wp-includes is a high-signal web shell drop for a core RCE that runs as the web user. Web-root paths are WordPress-specific, not a generic file-write template. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://www.cryptika.com/new-wp2shell-rce-vulnerability-hits-millions-of-wordpress-sites-emergency-patch-released/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress core auto-update to 6.9.5/7.0.2 rewriting bundled PHP files (expected right now given forced auto-updates)
  • Plugin/theme installation or update from the admin dashboard writing PHP into wp-content/plugins or /themes
  • Caching plugins (WP Super Cache/W3 Total Cache) generating advanced-cache.php or object-cache.php drop-ins
  • Backup/restore or staging-sync tooling repopulating the web root
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "wp-cron" and FolderPath !has "cache" and not (FileName in~ ("object-cache.php","advanced-cache.php","db.php"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the created file — flag short files containing eval/base64_decode/system/assert/$_REQUEST/$_POST/preg_replace(/e); compare the writer PID and timestamp against UC1 batch-endpoint requests and known update windows. 2) Contain: quarantine the file (do not delete before imaging), block web access to it, and isolate the host if the content is a shell. 3) Hunt: enumerate all files touched by the same PID/session, review access logs for GET/POST hits on the new filename, and check for scheduled tasks or wp_options/wp_users tampering.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/wp-content/","\\wp-content\\","/wp-admin/","\\wp-admin\\","/wp-includes/","\\wp-includes\\")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".php5" or FileName endswith ".php7" or FileName endswith ".phar"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, User=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, WebDaemon=InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/wp-content/","\\wp-content\\","/wp-admin/","\\wp-admin\\","/wp-includes/","\\wp-includes\\")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("php","phtml","php5","php7","phar")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Siemens ROX II: xz utility misused as 'cat' to read sensitive files (CVE-2025-40948) · [LLM] Ruggedcom ROX II firmware exposed to CVE-2025-40947/40948/40949 (below V2.17.1) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Siemens ROX II web management: shell metacharacters in HTTP requests (CVE-2025-40947/40949 command injection) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Siemens ROX II: malicious root cron entry via web task scheduler (CVE-2025-40949) · [LLM] Siemens ROX II: three-stage zero-day chain correlated on one device (CVE-2025-40948→40947→40949) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Siemens ROX II: xz utility misused as 'cat' to read sensitive files (CVE-2025-40948) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the CVE-2025-40948 arbitrary file disclosure primitive, where the root-privileged xz utility on a Ruggedcom ROX II switch is invoked with decompress-to-stdout flags against sensitive files (shadow, private keys, config) to function like cat. Article-specific because it keys on xz — not a generic file-read tool — reading credential/key material. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit CVE-2025-40948 mechanic: 'xz can be used with specific parameters to function like the standard Linux cat command' running as root to disclose 'password hashes and private cryptographic keys'. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty — Ruggedcom ROX II is an embedded OT switch with no EDR agent; only forwarded Syslog/auditd carries this. Cross-checked NVD and CISA ICS advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02 • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/siemens-rox-ii-zero-day-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005 T1006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin decompressing a .xz backup/log archive to stdout (but rarely against /etc/shadow or key paths)
  • Siemens support script bundling config for a support case
  • Firmware update tooling reading signed packages
  • Backup jobs streaming compressed config to a collector
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has '.xz' and SyslogMessage has_any ('/tmp/','/var/backup','/opt/backup'))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: On the flagged ROX II, confirm the xz invocation targeted /etc/shadow, SSH/private keys, or feature-key config, and identify the initiating session/user — legitimate decompression targets a .xz archive, not credential files. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the switch's management VLAN, rotate any exposed SSH host keys / device credentials, and force a config/credential reset; verify firmware is >= V2.17.1. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host/session for subsequent command-injection (feature key) and root cron writes — the next two stages of the chain.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName == 'xz' or SyslogMessage has 'xz '
| where SyslogMessage has_any ('-dc','--stdout','--decompress','-d ')
| where SyslogMessage has_any ('/etc/shadow','/etc/passwd','id_rsa','.pem','.key','/etc/ssh/','feature')
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Siemens ROX II web management: shell metacharacters in HTTP requests (CVE-2025-40947/40949 command injection) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the authenticated command-injection surface of Ruggedcom ROX II — the feature-key validation (CVE-2025-40947) and web task-scheduler (CVE-2025-40949) endpoints — by flagging HTTP requests to the switch's web management interface carrying shell metacharacters or command substitution. Article-specific: both flaws inject an attacker-controlled payload into a root-privileged command via the web GUI. Rationale: Both CVE-2025-40947 (feature key validation 'fails to sanitize an attacker-controlled payload before inserting it directly into a command executed with root privileges') and CVE-2025-40949 (scheduler 'improper input sanitization') are web-authenticated command injections, so shell metacharacters over HTTP to the mgmt GUI is the observable. Datadog/Falcon empty — no NGFW web source in scope; Defender empty (OT switch). Corroborated via NVD, which classes CVE-2025-40947 as authenticated command injection. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://windowsnews.ai/article/ruggedcom-rox-cve-2025-40947-siemens-patches-authenticated-command-injection-in-industrial-routers.418280 • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/siemens-rox-ii-zero-day-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate config values that legitimately contain '&' or ';' (e.g. URL query params, RADIUS strings) submitted via the GUI
  • Automated config-backup tooling POSTing complex payloads
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) probing the mgmt interface
  • Analyst penetration testing of the ROX II device
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ('Nessus','Qualys','Nuclei') or SourceIP in ('10.0.0.0'))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the flagged request's URL/body for genuine command substitution ($(...), backticks, ;id, |sh) vs. benign config characters, and check the HTTP response code — a 200 after an injection pattern suggests success. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP from the mgmt VLAN, capture the raw request, and confirm the ROX II firmware is patched to V2.17.1; disable the web GUI feature-key/scheduler endpoints if unpatched. 3) HUNT: On the same device, look for xz sensitive-file reads (stage 1) and new root cron entries (stage 3) within the following minutes.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ApplicationProtocol in ('HTTP','HTTPS') or isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestURL has_any (';','|','$(','`','&&','%3B','%7C','%24%28','%60','%26%26') or Message has_any ('$(','`;','|sh',';id','${IFS}')
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Siemens ROX II: malicious root cron entry via web task scheduler (CVE-2025-40949) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts CVE-2025-40949 persistence — the ROX II web management task scheduler injecting attacker commands into the root cron table, surviving reboot. Detects writes/modifications to root crontab paths on a ROX II device, especially when originating from the web management daemon rather than an interactive admin. Rationale: Directly maps CVE-2025-40949: 'inject malicious commands into the system's root cron table ... surviving system reboots'. Watches the exact persistence artifact (root crontab paths). Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty — OT switch, Syslog/auditd only. Datadog uses process/exec proxy since auditd source lacks a file-path facet. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/siemens-rox-ii-zero-day-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1053
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin scheduling a maintenance job via the ROX II scheduler GUI
  • Firmware update writing a post-boot cron hook
  • Siemens support adding a diagnostic cron entry
  • Monitoring agent installing a scheduled health check
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessName in ('dpkg','rpm','apt','yum') or SyslogMessage has 'siemens-firmware-update')
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Dump the current root crontab and cron.d contents on the flagged ROX II; compare the new entry's command against a known-good baseline — malicious entries typically call sh/curl/nc or reference /tmp payloads. 2) CONTAIN: Remove the unauthorized cron entry, isolate the mgmt VLAN, and confirm firmware is V2.17.1+; capture the entry for IR. 3) HUNT: Correlate backward for the preceding web command-injection request and xz file disclosure on the same host to confirm the full three-stage chain.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ('/etc/crontab','/etc/cron.d/','/var/spool/cron/crontabs/root','/var/spool/cron/root')
| where SyslogMessage has_any ('open','write','rename','create','O_WRONLY','O_CREAT') or Facility =~ 'cron'
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Siemens ROX II: three-stage zero-day chain correlated on one device (CVE-2025-40948→40947→40949) AIInstallation High
Correlation hunt that fires when a single ROX II switch exhibits multiple stages of the documented exploit chain within a short window — xz sensitive-file disclosure and/or web command injection followed by a root cron write. Confirms active exploitation of the full 'three steps to the terminal' chain rather than an isolated artifact. Rationale: Encodes the article's central thesis — a chained exploit ('Three Steps to the Terminal') — as temporal correlation of stage-1 xz disclosure and stage-3 root cron write on the same device within 15 minutes, which is far higher-fidelity than any single artifact. No Sigma (multi-event/temporal). Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty (OT switch, Syslog only). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/siemens-rox-ii-zero-day-vulnerabilities/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947
ATT&CKT1190 T1068 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Firmware upgrade window that both reads config (via xz) and installs cron hooks on the same device
  • Automated backup + scheduler-reconfiguration maintenance run
  • Vendor support session performing config export and job scheduling together
Suppression filter
| where Msg3 !has 'siemens-firmware-update' and Msg1 !has '/var/backup'
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Treat as high priority — pull all Syslog for the device across the 15-minute window and reconstruct the sequence (file read → cron write); validate whether a change window explains it. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the switch from OT and management networks, snapshot config, remove unauthorized cron entries, rotate device credentials/keys exposed in stage 1, and schedule firmware update to V2.17.1. 3) HUNT: Search other ROX II / Ruggedcom devices in the fleet for the same stage-1/stage-3 signatures and any lateral movement from the switch into HMI/PLC segments.
let win = 15m;
let filedisc = Syslog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where SyslogMessage has 'xz' and SyslogMessage has_any ('/etc/shadow','id_rsa','.pem','.key','/etc/ssh/')
  | project T1 = TimeGenerated, Computer, Stage1 = 'xz_file_read', Msg1 = SyslogMessage;
let cronwrite = Syslog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where SyslogMessage has_any ('/etc/crontab','/etc/cron.d/','/var/spool/cron/crontabs/root','/var/spool/cron/root')
  | project T3 = TimeGenerated, Computer, Stage3 = 'root_cron_write', Msg3 = SyslogMessage;
filedisc
| join kind=inner cronwrite on Computer
| where T3 between (T1 .. T1 + win)
| project Computer, T1, T3, ElapsedSec = datetime_diff('second', T3, T1), Stage1, Stage3, Msg1, Msg3
| sort by T1 desc

Ruggedcom ROX II firmware exposed to CVE-2025-40947/40948/40949 (below V2.17.1) AIReconnaissance Low
Inventory/exposure hunt that surfaces any managed asset reporting the three ROX II CVEs so the SOC can prioritise the V2.17.1 firmware update. Uses the exact CVE IDs and the fixed version named in the Siemens advisories. Rationale: Uses the most concrete strings in the article: the three CVE IDs and the fixed firmware V2.17.1 from Siemens advisories SSA-973901/SSA-078743/SSA-081142. Low confidence because Ruggedcom OT switches are frequently absent from TVM/scanner coverage; still the correct first defender action after a zero-day advisory. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch empty (not vuln-inventory sources here). Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02 • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/siemens-rox-ii-zero-day-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scanner mis-fingerprinting firmware version, flagging a device already on V2.17.1
  • Duplicate CMDB entries for the same physical switch
  • Decommissioned devices still in inventory
  • Non-ROX Ruggedcom models incorrectly mapped to these CVEs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the reported firmware is genuinely below V2.17.1 by querying the device directly; deduplicate against CMDB. 2) CONTAIN: For confirmed-vulnerable switches, restrict management-plane access (ACL the web GUI to a jump host, disable unused feature-key/scheduler functions) pending patch. 3) HUNT: Enable behavioral detections (xz file read, web command injection, root cron write) on the exposed devices and schedule the V2.17.1 update per Siemens SSA-973901/078743/081142.

ACR Stealer: Two observed intrusion chains amid increased threat activity

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-16 18 use cases 12 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

From late April 2026 to mid-June 2026, Microsoft Defender Experts observed increased ACR Stealer activity across customer environments. These campaigns are successfully using ClickFix lures to steal browser credentials, authentication tokens, and sensitive documents from enterprise environments. The post ACR Stealer: Two observed intrusion chains amid increased threat activity appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ClickFix RunMRU entry launching rundll32 against WebDAV GUID share (ACR Stealer) · [LLM] MSHTA remote HTA launched by explorer→powershell chain (ACR Stealer fileless campaign) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ACR Stealer: Two observed intrusion chains amid increased threat activity
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] rundll32 loading DLL from remote WebDAV @ssl GUID share with ordinal export (ACR Stealer) · [LLM] Masqueraded 'Autoupdate' scheduled task run by PowerShell loader (ACR Stealer persistence) · [LLM] pythonw.exe loader executing from deceptive %LocalAppData%\Temp dir (ACR Stealer) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint traffic to ACR Stealer C2 / dead-drop domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
ClickFix RunMRU entry launching rundll32 against WebDAV GUID share (ACR Stealer) AIDelivery High
Hunts the ACR Stealer ClickFix initial-access artifact: a Run-dialog (RunMRU) history value in which the pasted command drives cmd.exe/rundll32.exe to load a DLL from a remote WebDAV share addressed as a `@ssl` UNC path with a GUID directory. This is the on-disk fingerprint left when a victim pastes the ClickFix command, before any child process runs. Rationale: Anchors on the article's Block 1 RunMRU logic plus the corroborated `@ssl\<GUID>\` WebDAV UNC form; RunMRU only records manually pasted Run-dialog commands, so rundll32+@ssl+GUID there is near-zero-FP evidence of ClickFix paste-execution. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.gridinsoft.com/acr-stealer-clickfix-attacks/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4198788/new-acr-stealer-campaigns-use-webdav-mshta-to-evade-detection.html
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1218.011 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rare legitimate admin scripting that maps a WebDAV DAVWWWRoot share via rundll32 (uncommon in enterprise)
  • Security researcher / red team replaying the ClickFix chain in a sandbox
  • Backup or MDM tooling that writes synthetic RunMRU entries (very rare)
  • Manual analyst reproduction of the IOC on a triage box
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RegistryValueData and extract the WebDAV host + GUID; confirm it matches sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net or another external host, and check whether a rundll32.exe process with that UNC path actually spawned. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, block the WebDAV host/domain at proxy and DNS, and kill any rundll32/pythonw child processes. 3) Hunt: search the same host for the follow-on %LocalAppData%\Temp deceptive dir, the 'Autoupdate' scheduled task, and outbound traffic to the ACR C2 domains.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has "RunMRU"
| where RegistryValueData has_all ("rundll32", "@ssl")
| where RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)@ssl\\[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}\\"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("start", "pushd", ",#1", ".google")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has "RunMRU"
| where RegistryValueData has_all ("rundll32", "@ssl")
| where RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)@ssl\\[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}\\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

rundll32 loading DLL from remote WebDAV @ssl GUID share with ordinal export (ACR Stealer) AIInstallation High
Hunts the ACR Stealer campaign-1 execution step where rundll32.exe loads a DLL directly from a remote WebDAV share (UNC `\\host@SSL\<GUID>\<name>.google,#1`) over HTTPS. Matches the exact confirmed sample cmdline against sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net and the GUID directory + `,#1` ordinal export. Rationale: Uses the externally-confirmed exact cmdline shape (`rundll32.exe \\sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net\<GUID>\...google,#1`): rundll32 loading a DLL over a WebDAV @ssl UNC with a GUID dir and `,#N` ordinal export is not seen in benign activity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4198788/new-acr-stealer-campaigns-use-webdav-mshta-to-evade-detection.html • https://blog.gridinsoft.com/acr-stealer-clickfix-attacks/
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise apps that legitimately load resources from a mapped WebDAV/DAVWWWRoot path via rundll32 (rare)
  • Penetration test or purple-team replay of the ACR chain
  • Software installer that side-loads a DLL from an internal SharePoint WebDAV mount (would lack the external GUID host)
  • EDR sensor telemetry replays during IR reproduction
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the WebDAV host is external and non-corporate, capture the GUID path and DLL name, and check for a preceding cmd.exe/pushd parent and RunMRU paste. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the WebDAV domain/IP at proxy+DNS, and terminate rundll32 and any spawned pythonw.exe. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same GUID host or `,#1` ordinal pattern, and for the LogiOptionsPlus temp dir and 'Autoupdate' scheduled task on affected hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "rundll32.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i),#\d+\s*$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "@ssl" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net","creativecommunityinfo.art","enhanceblabber.cc","looksta.icu")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i),#\d+\s*$"
| where (CommandLine has "@ssl" or CommandLine has_any ("sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net","creativecommunityinfo.art","enhanceblabber.cc","looksta.icu"))
| where CommandLine matches regex @"[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MSHTA remote HTA launched by explorer→powershell chain (ACR Stealer fileless campaign) AIDelivery High
Hunts the ACR Stealer campaign-2 fileless chain: explorer.exe spawns a bare powershell.exe which invokes mshta.exe against a remote HTTPS URL whose path is a 7-digit numeric token. Matches the article's exact process-tree and cmdline shape for the MSHTA/steganography route. Rationale: Directly implements the article's Block 3 process-tree (explorer→powershell→mshta) plus the remote HTTPS HTA with a 7-digit path token; mshta fetching a remote URL from a PowerShell parent is a strong LOLBin proxy-execution signal specific to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/acr-stealer-uses-clickfix-lures-to.html • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4198788/new-acr-stealer-campaigns-use-webdav-mshta-to-evade-detection.html
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1059.001 T1204.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy internal LOB app delivered as a remote HTA via a launcher script (rare, and usually internal host not HTTPS/7-digit path)
  • Red-team ClickFix simulation
  • Admin troubleshooting that manually runs mshta against a URL
  • IT automation using mshta for a hosted config page
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the mshta URL, detonate/inspect it for the steganographic PNG stage, and confirm the explorer→powershell parentage indicates a paste-run rather than scripted automation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the HTA URL/domain, and kill mshta plus any in-memory child. 3) Hunt: look for follow-on obfuscated PowerShell, VirtualAlloc/Fiber-API in-memory execution, and browser credential-store access on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName has "explorer.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine in~ ('"PowerShell.exe" ', '"PowerShell.exe"')
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "https://" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex "/[0-9]{7}"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688

Masqueraded 'Autoupdate' scheduled task run by PowerShell loader (ACR Stealer persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the ACR Stealer campaign-1 persistence/updater behavior where the obfuscated PowerShell loader invokes schtasks to run a hidden task named 'Autoupdate' suffixed with an 8-digit numeric token, disguised as a legitimate software update triggering at user sign-in. Rationale: Implements the article's Block 2 exactly: a PowerShell parent driving schtasks against a task named 'Autoupdate' with an 8-digit token is a specific masqueraded-update persistence artifact, far narrower than generic scheduled-task creation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/microsoft-warns-of-surge-in-acr-stealer-attacks-on-customers/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.001 T1036
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software updaters that create tasks literally named 'Autoupdate' via a PowerShell installer (check the parent chain and signer)
  • Endpoint management/RMM tooling scripting scheduled tasks named with build numbers
  • Internal packaging scripts that name update tasks with date-stamps (8 digits)
  • Admin manually registering an update task through a PS console
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("AppData\\Local\\Temp", "pythonw", "LogiOptionsPlus")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full schtasks cmdline and the task action/trigger; confirm the action points to pythonw.exe or a %LocalAppData%\Temp path rather than a signed vendor binary. 2) Contain: delete the malicious task, isolate the host, and kill the associated pythonw/loader process. 3) Hunt: correlate to the upstream rundll32 WebDAV load and RunMRU paste, and check other hosts for identically-named 'Autoupdate'+8-digit tasks pointing into Temp.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("schtasks", "/tn", "Autoupdate")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex "[0-9]{8}"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has_all ("/tn", "Autoupdate")
| where CommandLine matches regex "[0-9]{8}"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

pythonw.exe loader executing from deceptive %LocalAppData%\Temp dir (ACR Stealer) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the ACR Stealer campaign-1 install step where a ZIP payload is extracted into a deceptive folder under %LocalAppData%\Temp (e.g. LogiOptionsPlus) and a bundled pythonw.exe is launched from that path by a PowerShell/cmd parent to run the obfuscated Python stealer loader with no console window. Rationale: Anchors on the article's install behavior: a bundled pythonw.exe run from a deceptive %LocalAppData%\Temp dir (e.g. LogiOptionsPlus) by a script-interpreter parent; console-less Python from Temp is atypical for legitimate deployed software. Cross-checked against: • https://socfortress.medium.com/acr-stealer-evolution-of-intrusion-chains-and-threat-activity-0052fb3dcc59
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1036.005 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PyInstaller-style apps or dev tooling that unpack an embedded Python into a Temp dir
  • CI/build agents invoking pythonw from a temp working directory
  • Vendor telemetry agents bundling their own Python runtime under LocalAppData
  • Data-science users running notebook helpers from Temp
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-enc", "IEX", "DownloadString", "FromBase64String", "Expand-Archive")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the pythonw folder path and sibling files; look for an archive/installer masquerade, a bundled interpreter, and whether the parent PowerShell was the obfuscated loader. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill pythonw and any injected system process, and quarantine the Temp deceptive directory. 3) Hunt: check for VirtualAlloc/Fiber-API in-memory injection, DPAPI browser-store access, and the 'Autoupdate' scheduled task on the same and neighboring hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pythonw.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Temp\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\pythonw.exe"
| where NewProcessName has @"\AppData\Local\Temp\"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint traffic to ACR Stealer C2 / dead-drop domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections or DNS lookups to the corroborated ACR Stealer campaign infrastructure (creativecommunityinfo.art, enhanceblabber.cc, sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net, looksta.icu, claude-desktop.gitlab.io) used for WebDAV payload staging and C2 resolution. Rationale: Pre-extracted campaign domains, with sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net independently confirmed as the WebDAV staging host in external write-ups; direct IOC hits on these domains are high-fidelity for this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4198788/new-acr-stealer-campaigns-use-webdav-mshta-to-evade-detection.html • https://blog.gridinsoft.com/acr-stealer-clickfix-attacks/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed crawler or sandbox in the environment resolving the IOC domains
  • Security researcher browsing the C2 domains from a corp host
  • Proxy/DNS logging replayed during IR that re-surfaces historical lookups
  • Domain sinkhole/monitoring service inside the org
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process for the connection/lookup (rundll32, pythonw, mshta, powershell) and confirm it is not a known security tool. 2) Contain: block all five domains at DNS+proxy, isolate any host that resolved them, and capture memory before reimage. 3) Hunt: pivot from the host to the full ACR chain (RunMRU paste, WebDAV rundll32 load, Autoupdate task, browser-credential access) and check for stolen-token reuse in Entra/M365 sign-in logs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("creativecommunityinfo.art","enhanceblabber.cc","sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net","looksta.icu","claude-desktop.gitlab.io")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let acrDomains = dynamic(["creativecommunityinfo.art","enhanceblabber.cc","sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net","looksta.icu","claude-desktop.gitlab.io"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (acrDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
