HelloNet C2 egress to 5.39.253.206 / 176.32.34.135 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any outbound connection to the two confirmed HelloNet command-and-control IPs (5.39.253.206 — also the SSH tunnel endpoint on 3522 — and 176.32.34.135). A flat IOC-match detection to catch beacon, tunnel, or proxy traffic regardless of the originating process. Rationale: Two hard network IOCs named in the article; 5.39.253.206 is doubly confirmed as both the SSH-tunnel endpoint (port 3522) and the proxy C2. Flat IOC match, alerting tier. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanner or sandbox detonating the sample from a corporate range (whitelist known research hosts)
  • Security appliance actively probing the C2 for enrichment
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse if the adversary infrastructure is later repurposed (validate against current IOC feeds)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the InitiatingProcess and port — svchost/frontpage.exe on 5003 or 3522 strongly confirms HelloNet; a browser hit may be incidental. 2) CONTAIN: block both IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, and capture netflow for scoping. 3) HUNT: enumerate every internal host that contacted either IP, then pivot to UC1 (side-load), UC3 (tesh4RPC.txt), and UC6 (svchost listeners) on each.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("5.39.253.206", "176.32.34.135")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("5.39.253.206", "176.32.34.135")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HelloProxy listener: svchost.exe binding TCP 5003/5060 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the injected HelloProxy component, which after hooking AFD listens on ports 5003 and 5060 inside svchost.exe awaiting C2 commands. A svchost process creating a listening socket on these non-standard ports is highly anomalous. Rationale: Article states HelloProxy 'starts listening on ports 5003 and 5060' from within svchost after injection. svchost.exe is not a normal listener on these ports. Sentinel/Sigma/Datadog/Falcon omitted: none of the tenant-available tables cleanly express a Windows listening-socket-created event (Sysmon does not emit listeners by default; ImNetworkSession lacks listener semantics), so this is deliberately Defender-native. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1571 T1090.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine SIP/VoIP service or softphone binding 5060 (verify hosting process is not svchost -netsvcs)
  • Legitimate service hosted in svchost that a third-party product registered on 5003
  • Port-reuse by an unrelated internal application after the malicious process exits
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\System32\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "netsvcs"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm the listening svchost's command line is the -netsvcs variant and check for the sibling wtsapi32.dll side-load (UC1) and tesh4RPC.txt (UC3) on the host. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the host, capture a memory image of the svchost (HelloProxy runs in memory), then suspend/kill it and block the C2 IPs. 3) HUNT: sweep for any svchost listening on 5003/5060 fleet-wide and correlate with inbound connections to those ports and outbound to 5.39.253.206/176.32.34.135.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort in (5003, 5060)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalPort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort in (5003, 5060)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, LocalPort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (5003,5060) All_Traffic.process_name="svchost.exe" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (5003,5060) All_Traffic.process_name="svchost.exe" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or SHA1 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or MD5 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or SHA1 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or MD5 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent: a persistent threat evolves with sophisticated data collection and exfiltration

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-16 9 use cases 6 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Two-phase attacks with the GoSerpent backdoor, Stowaway RAT, ThumbcacheService and other tools aim to steal data from government entities in Southeast Asia.

ATT&CKT1003 T1003.001 T1027 T1190 T1204.002 T1558

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GoSerpent: a persistent threat evolves with sophisticated data collection and ex
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GoSerpent/McMx masquerading proxy binaries lass.exe and updates.exe · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GoSerpent ThumbcacheService staging DB (thumbcache_605a.db) written to C:\Users\Public · [LLM] GoSerpent 7-Zip archiving with hardcoded campaign password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# · [LLM] GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash / SAM hive local hash extraction · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
GoSerpent ThumbcacheService staging DB (thumbcache_605a.db) written to C:\Users\Public AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts creation of the ThumbcacheService collection database thumbcache_605a.db in C:\Users\Public\, where GoSerpent stages harvested .doc/.docx/.pdf/.xls/.xlsx documents before exfiltration. Legitimate Windows thumbnail caches use the same thumbcache_*.db naming but live under AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer, never in the Public profile, making the Public-path variant article-specific. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim filename thumbcache_605a.db (code block) and the C:\Users\Public\ staging path; legitimate thumbcache DBs never live in the Public profile, so the path variant catches renamed samples with near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1119
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user or admin manually copying their AppData thumbnail cache into C:\Users\Public for troubleshooting
  • Backup/migration tooling that mirrors user profile Explorer caches into a shared Public folder
  • Forensic/IR tools exporting thumbcache artifacts to C:\Users\Public for analysis
  • A security researcher detonating the sample in a lab on a monitored host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\explorer.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName that wrote the DB; a service DLL host (svchost.exe hosting an unknown service) or a binary in Public/Temp is high-suspicion. Inspect the file for a 7-Zip archive nearby and confirm it is not a genuine Explorer cache. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture the DB and any adjacent .7z archives for analysis, and disable/stop the suspicious Windows service backing ThumbcacheService. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for 7-Zip archiving with the campaign password, lass.exe/updates.exe processes, and SAM/LSASS credential-dumping activity in the prior days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "thumbcache_605a.db"
    or (FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\" and FileName startswith "thumbcache_" and FileName endswith ".db")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "thumbcache_605a.db"
    or (TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public\" and TargetFileName startswith "thumbcache_" and TargetFileName endswith ".db")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GoSerpent ThumbcacheService Staging Database Created
id: 8f2c1a4e-7b93-4d21-9c6a-1e0f5b2d3a44
description: Detects creation of the ThumbcacheService collection DB thumbcache_605a.db used by the GoSerpent backdoor to stage stolen documents.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.collection
  - attack.t1074.001
  - attack.t1119
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_name:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\thumbcache_605a.db'
  selection_public:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\Users\Public\'
    TargetFilename|contains: '\thumbcache_'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.db'
  condition: selection_name or selection_public
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\thumbcache_605a.db OR *\Thumbcache_605a.db OR *\THUMBCACHE_605A.DB OR *\Users\Public\thumbcache_*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/thumbcache_605a\.db$/i OR TargetFileName=/\\Users\\Public\\thumbcache_.*\.db$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="thumbcache_605a.db" OR (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Users\\Public\\*" AND Filesystem.file_name="thumbcache_*.db")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="thumbcache_605a.db" OR (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Users\\Public\\*" AND Filesystem.file_name="thumbcache_*.db")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
GoSerpent 7-Zip archiving with hardcoded campaign password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts ThumbcacheService's 7-Zip archiving stage, which packs collected documents into password-protected archives using the fixed password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# with a 20MB volume limit. The password string is a unique campaign artifact, so any command line containing it is effectively a signature regardless of the archiver binary name. Rationale: The password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# is a verbatim campaign string with effectively zero legitimate use; matching its alphanumeric core (vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6) survives quoting/escaping and catches renamed 7z binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst re-running the sample's archive command during malware analysis on a lab host
  • Threat-intel/IR playbook that references the password string in a script comment for testing detections
  • Purple-team exercise emulating GoSerpent's archiving stage
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the archiver binary (7z.exe/7za.exe or a renamed copy) and the target file set; look for the -v20m volume flag and the source documents being packed. 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the produced archives, and block outbound to any network share the archives were destined for. 3) Hunt: locate thumbcache_605a.db on the same host, review the credential-dumping activity that supplied the share credentials, and check network-share write events for exfiltration of the archives.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent/McMx masquerading proxy binaries lass.exe and updates.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of GoSerpent's masquerading binaries lass.exe (mimicking lsass.exe) and updates.exe, which host the SOCKS5 proxy/RAT. lass.exe is never a legitimate Windows binary, and updates.exe running from user-writable/staging directories is a strong anomaly for this campaign. Rationale: lass.exe and updates.exe are named verbatim in the article (code blocks) as GoSerpent's process-masquerading filenames; lass.exe has no legitimate counterpart and the path constraint on updates.exe filters the common legitimate updater binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1090.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party application shipping its own updates.exe from ProgramData/AppData (e.g. some auto-updaters)
  • Developer/test binary coincidentally named lass.exe in a source tree
  • Software packaging or installer temp extraction dropping an updates.exe into a Temp directory
  • Portable app launched from a USB/Public share named updates.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "updates.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and signer of the process; unsigned lass.exe or a Go-compiled updates.exe from a user-writable path is high-confidence. Check for a listening socket / SOCKS5 behavior and outbound C2 from the same PID. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and block the associated C2 IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: search for ThumbcacheService staging (thumbcache_605a.db), the 7-Zip archive password, and credential-dumping tools deployed by the same backdoor across the environment.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "lass.exe"
    or (FileName =~ "updates.exe" and FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith @"\lass.exe" or TargetProcessName =~ "lass.exe"
    or ((TargetProcessName endswith @"\updates.exe" or TargetProcessName =~ "updates.exe") and TargetProcessName has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash / SAM hive local hash extraction AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the QuarksDumpLocalHash tool GoSerpent deploys to extract local account password hashes from the SAM registry hive for offline cracking, plus the equivalent reg.exe SAM/SECURITY hive save. This is distinct from LSASS memory access and targets the on-disk SAM credential store. Rationale: Anchored on the named tool QuarksDumpLocalHash and its documented SAM-hive extraction behavior; the reg.exe hive-save branch catches the same TTP if the operator uses a LOLBin instead of the custom tool, and it deliberately avoids overlapping the existing LSASS-access detection. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1003.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin exporting a SAM/SECURITY hive for legitimate password-audit or migration tooling
  • Endpoint hardening/audit software (e.g. compliance scanners) reading local hive backups
  • IR/forensics collection scripts that reg save HKLM\SAM for evidence
  • Backup software snapshotting registry hives
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("forensic_collector.exe","psexec.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cmd.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "backup")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent process and account; a hive save or quarks* binary spawned by an unknown Go backdoor (lass.exe/updates.exe) rather than an admin session is high-confidence. Check whether the resulting hive/hash output was written to a staging path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-reset local account passwords (and any domain accounts used interactively), and revoke cached credentials. 3) Hunt: correlate with ThumbcacheService staging and network-share writes — the dumped credentials are used to authenticate to shares for exfiltration; review share-access logs for the affected accounts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName has "quarks" or ProcessCommandLine has "QuarksDumpLocalHash"
    or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "save" and ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"hklm\sam", @"hklm\security"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "quarks" or CommandLine has "QuarksDumpLocalHash"
    or (NewProcessName endswith @"\reg.exe" and CommandLine has "save" and (CommandLine has @"hklm\sam" or CommandLine has @"hklm\security"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash SAM Hive Dump
id: d70e2b19-3c84-4a56-b0f1-9a2c4e7d6b12
description: Detects QuarksDumpLocalHash or reg.exe saving the SAM/SECURITY hive to extract local password hashes, as deployed by the GoSerpent backdoor.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_tool:
    CommandLine|contains: 'QuarksDumpLocalHash'
  selection_toolname:
    Image|contains: 'quarks'
  selection_regsave:
    Image|endswith: '\reg.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'save'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'hklm\sam'
      - 'hklm\security'

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\QuarksDumpLocalHash.exe OR *\quarksdumplocalhash.exe) OR @CommandLine:(*QuarksDumpLocalHash* OR *quarksdumplocalhash*) OR (@Image:(*\reg.exe OR *\REG.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*save* OR *SAVE*) AND @CommandLine:(*HKLM\SAM* OR *hklm\sam* OR *HKLM\SECURITY* OR *hklm\security*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/quarks/i OR CommandLine=/QuarksDumpLocalHash/i OR (ImageFileName=/\\reg\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/save/i AND CommandLine=/hklm\\(sam|security)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="*quarks*" OR Processes.process="*QuarksDumpLocalHash*" OR (Processes.process_name="reg.exe" AND Processes.process="*save*" AND (Processes.process="*hklm\\sam*" OR Processes.process="*hklm\\security*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="*quarks*" OR Processes.process="*QuarksDumpLocalHash*" OR (Processes.process_name="reg.exe" AND Processes.process="*save*" AND (Processes.process="*hklm\\sam*" OR Processes.process="*hklm\\security*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UAT-11795 weaponized HTA delivery via mshta.exe from ClickFix staging domain AIDelivery High
Hunts mshta.exe launching a remote/local HTA stager, the article-described entry point for UAT-11795 (weaponized HTA downloader delivered via a likely ClickFix technique from zynaris[.]io). Flags mshta invocations carrying a URL/.hta argument, especially referencing the campaign staging domain, and their child installer/PowerShell spawns. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated entry point (mshta.exe HTA downloader via ClickFix) and the campaign staging domain zynaris[.]io; mshta with a remote/.hta argument is rare in benign user activity, making it high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1566.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy enterprise apps that still ship .hta admin utilities launched via mshta
  • IT automation/logon scripts invoking mshta with an internal http path
  • Software packaging tools (SCCM/Intune) that stage .hta helpers
  • Developer testing of HTA content locally
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\CCM" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the mshta command line and resolve the URL host — confirm whether it is zynaris[.]io or another external/unfamiliar domain vs an internal IT resource. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the staging domain at proxy/DNS, and capture the downloaded HTA/installer from %TEMP% for analysis. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for follow-on trojanized installer execution (MobaXterm/WebEx/Zoom/DBeaver/FaceIT), python.exe spawns from PythonLauncher-* folders, and outbound to windowscreenrepairnearme[.]com / aipythondevs[.]com.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("zynaris.io", ".hta", "http://", "https://", "javascript:", "vbscript:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          MshtaCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has_any ("zynaris.io", ".hta", "http://", "https://", "javascript:", "vbscript:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UAT-11795 trojanized installer spawns Python bytecode loader (PythonLauncher-*) AIInstallation High
Hunts trojanized software installers (MobaXterm, WebEx, Zoom, DBeaver, FACEIT) whose NSIS package spawns byte-compiled Python that loads Starland RAT in memory. Anchors on the exact installer filenames from the article and the PythonLauncher-{3 random chars} working folder plus Telegram bot beacon traffic. Rationale: Uses the exact trojanized installer filenames (MobaXterm_v26.1.exe etc.) and the article's PythonLauncher-{3 random chars} loader artifact; a signed-looking installer spawning a Python interpreter is anomalous and campaign-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195532/malware/new-russian-campaign-uses-fake-webex-and-zoom-installers-to-deploy-starland-rat.html
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Python-based installers or apps that bundle an embedded interpreter
  • Developer machines where DBeaver/other tools genuinely launch Python plugins
  • Software distribution repackaging that wraps installers and calls python
  • Data-science tooling installers extracting to random temp folders
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the installer file's origin (download URL/referrer) and digital signature; genuine vendor installers are signed and do not spawn python.exe. Capture the PythonLauncher-* folder contents. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the installer and Python artifacts, and block the download source. 3) Hunt: check the host for outbound to api.telegram.org (bots 8384531459 / 7993597060), Starland C2 domains, and CastleStealer/Remcos follow-on shellcode execution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MobaXterm_v26.1.exe","WebEx_Client.exe","dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe","FaceitInstaller_x64.exe","Zoom installer.exe")
     or ProcessCommandLine has "PythonLauncher-"
     or FolderPath has "PythonLauncher-"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Installer = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InstallerCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          PyImage = FolderPath,
          PyCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\python.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pythonw.exe"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("MobaXterm_v26.1.exe","WebEx_Client.exe","dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe","FaceitInstaller_x64.exe")
     or CommandLine has "PythonLauncher-"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Starland RAT HWID C2 beaconing from Python process AICommand & Control High
Detects Starland RAT command-and-control: a python.exe/pythonw.exe process making outbound connections to the primary Starland C2 domains windowscreenrepairnearme[.]com and aipythondevs[.]com, whose URLs embed a per-victim C: drive volume serial number as the final path component. High-fidelity because a Python interpreter beaconing to these specific domains is not benign. Rationale: Anchors on the two named primary Starland RAT C2 domains and the article's per-victim volume-serial URL scheme, initiated specifically by a Python interpreter — the combination is not observed in benign traffic. Sentinel query uses ImWebSession host/URL fields (no process column exists on that table). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://gbhackers.com/starland-rat-steals-browser-credentials/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher/sandbox detonation of the sample generating C2 traffic
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving/curling the IOC domains
  • Proxy prefetch/URL-scanning appliances touching the domain
  • A future benign re-registration of a lapsed hijacked domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Anaconda3\\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pip install"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is a Python interpreter and extract the full URL — the trailing hex segment is the victim volume serial (unique fingerprint). 2) Contain: isolate the host, sinkhole/block windowscreenrepairnearme[.]com and aipythondevs[.]com, and kill the python process tree. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for the Polygon smart-contract fallback (Eth_call / 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba), staging-domain traffic to eorthopaedics[.]com/sastoro[.]com /feed/ and /alpha/, and browser/wallet file access.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("windowscreenrepairnearme.com","aipythondevs.com")
     or RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)(windowscreenrepairnearme|aipythondevs)\.com/.+/[0-9A-Fa-f]{8}$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstHostname has_any ("windowscreenrepairnearme.com","aipythondevs.com")
     or Url has_any ("windowscreenrepairnearme.com","aipythondevs.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstHostname, Url, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UAT-11795 staging chain + WLDR PowerShell C2 over /feed/ and /alpha/ paths AICommand & Control High
Detects the UAT-11795 PowerShell stage chain and parallel WLDR C2: PowerShell (or other host) retrieving payloads from eorthopaedics[.]com and sastoro[.]com under the article-specific /feed/ and /alpha/ URL paths that carry HWID-parameterized encrypted envelopes. Targets both the staging download and the persistent WLDR beacon. Rationale: Uses the two named staging/parallel-C2 domains plus the article's distinctive /feed/ and /alpha/ routing paths that carry HWID-encrypted envelopes — the host+path combination is a precise campaign fingerprint that avoids matching the domains' legitimate content. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://cyberpress.org/uat-11795-spreads-dual-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate visitors to eorthopaedics[.]com (a likely hijacked but otherwise real site) hitting unrelated pages — mitigated by the /feed//alpha/ path requirement
  • Security tooling crawling the domains for IOC validation
  • Proxy URL-rewrite that appends /feed/ style paths
  • RSS/feed readers coincidentally polling a /feed/ path on these hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and inspect the full URL — a hex/HWID trailing component under /feed/ or /alpha/ confirms the WLDR envelope. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block eorthopaedics[.]com and sastoro[.]com, and capture the PowerShell stager from memory/disk. 3) Hunt: look for the WLDR Runspace loader, New-ScheduledTask persistence, and correlate with Starland RAT beacons to windowscreenrepairnearme[.]com / aipythondevs[.]com on the same or related hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com")
| where RemoteUrl has "/feed/" or RemoteUrl has "/alpha/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DstHostname in~ ("eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com") or Url has_any ("eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com"))
| where Url has "/feed/" or Url has "/alpha/"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstHostname, Url, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Starland RAT Polygon smart-contract fallback C2 resolution (Eth_call) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects Starland RAT's resilient fallback channel: retrieval of an XOR-encrypted backup C2 domain from the Polygon smart contract 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba via a public JSON-RPC Eth_call. Anchors on the exact contract address string and Polygon RPC endpoints appearing in process/script activity or outbound traffic. Rationale: The contract address 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba is a unique, article-specific string; combined with eth_call to Polygon RPC by a python/powershell process it is an unambiguous fallback-C2 indicator. Medium confidence because obfuscation may hide the literal string, so the network-to-Polygon-RPC leg is included. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/
ATT&CKT1102 T1568
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate blockchain developers/wallet apps making eth_call to polygon-rpc.com
  • Crypto trading bots or DeFi tooling on the endpoint
  • Node/Python web3 libraries in a dev environment querying Polygon
  • Browser extensions (MetaMask) proxying RPC — though those rarely appear as python/powershell initiators
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process — a python/powershell interpreter querying Polygon RPC or embedding the contract address is not typical business use; check the host for Starland RAT artifacts. 2) Contain: isolate the host and block polygon-rpc.com egress for that process; the fallback resolves the next C2 so also block primary/staging domains. 3) Hunt: decode any XOR-encrypted domain returned and add it to blocklists; sweep the estate for the same contract-address string or eth_call pattern from non-developer hosts.
union
(
  DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba","eth_call","polygon-rpc.com","rpc.ankr.com/polygon")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source="Process", FileName, Detail=ProcessCommandLine
),
(
  DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has_any ("polygon-rpc.com","rpc.ankr.com","polygon-mainnet")
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="Network", FileName=InitiatingProcessFileName, Detail=RemoteUrl
)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstHostname has_any ("polygon-rpc.com","rpc.ankr.com","polygon-mainnet") or Url has_any ("polygon-rpc.com","rpc.ankr.com","0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Starland RAT browser credential & cryptocurrency wallet harvesting via Python AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Starland RAT / CastleStealer collection stage: a python.exe/pythonw.exe (or PythonLauncher-*) process reading browser profile stores (Chrome/Edge/Firefox Login Data) and cryptocurrency wallet directories. Article states the RAT steals browser data and crypto wallets; corroborating reporting notes 40+ wallet targets. Rationale: Combines the article's stated collection behaviour (browser data + crypto wallets) with the campaign's Python execution vector; requiring a Python interpreter to touch >=2 distinct credential/wallet stores raises fidelity over a generic browser-file-access rule. Wallet target breadth corroborated by external reporting (40+ wallets). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://gbhackers.com/starland-rat-steals-browser-credentials/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Python-based backup/migration scripts copying browser profiles
  • Security tooling or DFIR scripts collecting browser artifacts
  • Developer test automation (Selenium/Playwright) reading browser profiles
  • Password-manager import utilities written in Python touching Login Data
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Anaconda3\\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("selenium","playwright","backup")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Python process lineage (was it spawned by a trojanized installer / PythonLauncher-*?) and enumerate exactly which browser/wallet stores were read. 2) Contain: isolate the host and force-reset credentials for accounts stored in the affected browsers; advise the user to move any crypto wallet funds from a clean device. 3) Hunt: correlate with Starland C2 beacons and Telegram exfil (bots 8384531459 / 7993597060), and search for CastleStealer .NET stealer or Remcos artifacts as follow-on payloads.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "PythonLauncher-"
| where FolderPath has_any (
    @"\User Data\", "Login Data", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\",
    @"\Exodus\", @"\Ethereum\", @"\Electrum\", "wallet.dat", @"\Bitcoin\", "web3")
| summarize PathsTouched = dcount(FolderPath), SamplePaths = make_set(FolderPath, 12), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId
| where PathsTouched >= 2   // 2 = require multiple sensitive stores, not a single incidental hit
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe") or ActingProcessName has "PythonLauncher-"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\User Data\\", "Login Data", "\\Mozilla\\Firefox\\Profiles\\", "\\Exodus\\", "\\Ethereum\\", "\\Electrum\\", "wallet.dat", "\\Bitcoin\\")
| summarize PathsTouched = dcount(TargetFilePath), SamplePaths = make_set(TargetFilePath, 12), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
          by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId
| where PathsTouched >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\python.exe OR *\pythonw.exe OR *\PYTHON.EXE) (@TargetFilename:*\User\ Data\* OR @TargetFilename:*Login\ Data* OR @TargetFilename:*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\* OR @TargetFilename:*\Exodus\* OR @TargetFilename:*\Ethereum\* OR @TargetFilename:*wallet.dat*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/\\pythonw?\.exe$/i
| regex("(\\\\User Data\\\\|Login Data|\\\\Mozilla\\\\Firefox\\\\Profiles\\\\|\\\\Exodus\\\\|\\\\Ethereum\\\\|wallet\.dat|\\\\Electrum\\\\)", field=TargetFileName, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN (python.exe,pythonw.exe) AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\User Data\\*Login Data*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Mozilla\\Firefox\\Profiles\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Ethereum\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Exodus\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*wallet*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN (python.exe,pythonw.exe) AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\User Data\\*Login Data*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Mozilla\\Firefox\\Profiles\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Ethereum\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Exodus\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*wallet*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Unpacking the AsyncAPI npm supply chain compromise and import-time payload delivery

Microsoft Security BlogStepSecurity
2026-07-16 18 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors compromised AsyncAPI packages and weaponized trusted CI/CD workflows to distribute malware through npm. This analysis breaks down the attack chain, payload delivery, and recommended defenses. The post Unpacking the AsyncAPI npm supply chain compromise and import-time payload delivery appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised @asyncapi npm package versions resolved into node_modules / Yarn cache · [LLM] Node.js retrieving Miasma second stage from IPFS gateway (specific CIDs) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Unpacking the AsyncAPI npm supply chain compromise and import-time payload deliv
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Second-stage sync.js dropped under OS 'NodeJS' masquerade directory · [LLM] Detached hidden node.exe executing sync.js from NodeJS masquerade path
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to Miasma controller 85.137.53.71 on ports 8080/8081/8091 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Compromised @asyncapi npm package versions resolved into node_modules / Yarn cache AIDelivery High
Hunts for the five backdoored @asyncapi package versions (@asyncapi/specs 6.11.2 & 6.11.2-alpha.1, generator 3.3.1, generator-components 0.7.1, generator-helpers 1.1.1) landing on developer/CI hosts via npm or Yarn dependency resolution. Article-specific because it pins the exact malicious name+version pairs Microsoft/Socket confirmed, not generic 'npm install' activity. Rationale: Anchors on the exact malicious name+version pairs Microsoft published and Socket/StepSecurity independently confirmed; package name is always lowercase in the registry/cache so no casing enumeration needed, and version+name combined is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages.html
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers or IR teams intentionally downloading the malicious versions into a sandbox for analysis
  • An internal mirror/Artifactory that cached the bad versions during the exposure window and is now being audited
  • Developers who pinned 6.11.2 in a lockfile and re-ran install against a still-poisoned private proxy
  • Yarn/npm cache directories restored from an old backup image containing the version
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","yarn.exe","npm-cli.js") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("malware-analysis","sandbox","detonate"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path is a real install target (node_modules, .yarn/cache, npm _cacache) and not a knowingly-collected sample; capture the host, user, and whether it's a dev box or CI runner. 2) Contain: isolate the host, purge npm & Yarn caches, remove all five affected versions, and pin @asyncapi/specs to a known-good release; block 85.137.53.71:8080/8081/8091 at egress. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to a detached node child writing sync.js under the NodeJS masquerade dir and any outbound IPFS fetch; rotate every credential reachable from that environment (npm tokens, GitHub CLI, AWS, SSH keys).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName has "asyncapi"
| where (FileName has "specs" and FileName has "6.11.2")
    or (FileName has "generator-helpers" and FileName has "1.1.1")
    or (FileName has "generator-components" and FileName has "0.7.1")
    or (FileName has "generator" and FileName has "3.3.1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName has "asyncapi"
| where (TargetFileName has "specs" and TargetFileName has "6.11.2")
    or (TargetFileName has "generator-helpers" and TargetFileName has "1.1.1")
    or (TargetFileName has "generator-components" and TargetFileName has "0.7.1")
    or (TargetFileName has "generator" and TargetFileName has "3.3.1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Backdoored @asyncapi npm package version written to disk
id: 6f2c1a90-4b3e-4d21-9e77-2a1f5c8e0a11
description: Detects the exact malicious @asyncapi package+version tarballs/files from the July 2026 npm supply-chain compromise landing in node_modules or package-manager caches.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/15/unpacking-asyncapi-npm-supply-chain-compromise-import-time-payload-delivery/

Second-stage sync.js dropped under OS 'NodeJS' masquerade directory AIInstallation High
Detects the import-time loader writing its IPFS-fetched second stage as sync.js into the OS-specific NodeJS masquerade folder (%LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS, ~/Library/Application Support/NodeJS, ~/.local/share/NodeJS, ~/.config/NodeJS). Article-specific: the fixed filename sync.js plus the fake NodeJS directory is a unique fingerprint of this campaign, not generic file drops. Rationale: Uses the verbatim FILE_NAME='sync.js' constant and the getTargetDirectory() 'NodeJS' masquerade paths from the article's code block 2 — the combination is unique to this loader and confirmed by Microsoft's own Query 1. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool that genuinely names its data dir 'NodeJS' and writes a sync.js sync script
  • Developer scaffolding/boilerplate that creates a sync.js worker under an app-support folder
  • A backup/restore of a previously-infected profile re-materializing sync.js
  • Security tooling replaying the sample into a NodeJS folder during analysis
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "npm" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "yarn"
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash sync.js and check its parent process — a node.exe/node child with detached/hidden flags confirms; benign scripts have a real signed parent. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the detached node process tree, delete sync.js, and block 85.137.53.71:8080/8081/8091 plus ipfs.io retrieval at egress. 3) Hunt: pivot to which @asyncapi version installed on the host, look for outbound IPFS CID fetches (Qmet4… / QmQobZSp…), and rotate all credentials reachable from the environment given Miasma's credential-harvest module.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "sync.js"
| where FolderPath has "NodeJS"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "sync.js"
| where TargetFilePath has "NodeJS"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detached hidden node.exe executing sync.js from NodeJS masquerade path AIInstallation High
Detects the import-time payload's execution stage: a node process launching the dropped sync.js out of the NodeJS masquerade directory, matching the spawn('node',[payloadPath],{detached,stdio:ignore,windowsHide}) pattern. Article-specific via the sync.js + NodeJS command-line pairing (mirrors Microsoft's published hunting Query 1). Rationale: Combines the verbatim FILE_NAME 'sync.js' and 'NodeJS' masquerade path from code block 2 with a node interpreter parent — the same signal Microsoft ships as their behavioral coverage for the detached Node.js spawn. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/asyncapi-npm-packages-backdoored-via-github-actions
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1564.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An in-house Node app that happens to keep a sync.js worker inside a directory literally named NodeJS
  • Electron/CLI tooling that stores helper scripts under an app-support NodeJS folder
  • Analyst detonation of the sample in a sandbox VM
  • A monorepo build task named sync.js executed with a NodeJS-prefixed cwd
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jest","webpack","vite","--build") and DeviceName has "build")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the full command line and grandparent — a build/import node.exe (from npm/yarn) spawning this detached child confirms the chain; note the SHA256 of sync.js. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the detached node tree, remove sync.js, and block the C2 IP/ports and IPFS egress. 3) Hunt: correlate to the affected @asyncapi version on the host and any outbound connection to 85.137.53.71 or ipfs.io CIDs within minutes; force credential rotation for npm/GitHub/AWS/SSH accessible from that host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "node"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "sync.js"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "NodeJS"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine

Outbound C2 to Miasma controller 85.137.53.71 on ports 8080/8081/8091 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the Miasma runtime's command-and-control beaconing to the hardcoded controller 85.137.53.71 over its three fixed ports. Article-specific: a single named IP plus the exact non-standard port trio Microsoft told orgs to block — near-zero ambiguity. Rationale: Single hardcoded controller IP plus the exact port trio (8080/8081/8091) that Microsoft explicitly recommended blocking — a definitive C2 indicator with essentially no legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-asyncapi-npm-supply-chain-attack-delivers-multi-stage-miasma-botnet-via-compromised-github-act • https://www.ox.security/blog/asyncapi-npm-organization-compromised-2m-weekly-downloads-affected/
ATT&CKT1571 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel/IR analyst deliberately connecting to the C2 for characterization from a sanctioned sandbox
  • A honeypot or deception host configured to beacon to known-bad IPs
  • Vulnerability scanner probing the IP as part of an external asset sweep
  • Reuse of 85.137.53.71 by an unrelated benign service after takedown (verify recency)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — node.exe/sync.js confirms Miasma; capture host, user, and beacon cadence. 2) Contain: isolate host, block 85.137.53.71 on 8080/8081/8091 at perimeter and host firewall, and kill the responsible process tree. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the same IP/ports and for the decentralized fallback channels (Nostr, Ethereum, BitTorrent DHT, libp2p, IPFS); enumerate which imported @asyncapi and rotate every reachable credential.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "85.137.53.71"
| where RemotePort in (8080, 8081, 8091)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "85.137.53.71"
| where DstPortNumber in (8080, 8081, 8091)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DstDomain
| order by TimeGenerated desc
