Node.js retrieving Miasma second stage from IPFS gateway (specific CIDs) AIDelivery High
Detects the child loader fetching sync.js from IPFS via ipfs.io, keyed on the two campaign CIDs (Qmet4fhsAaWMBUxNDfREHwgiyDeSWy4YSYs9wiKUW5jGyf for specs, QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9 for the generator family) or any node process hitting the ipfs.io gateway. Article-specific via the exact IPFS content identifiers. Rationale: Uses the two verbatim IPFS CIDs from the article's Table 2 and the ipfs.io gateway constant from code block 2; a node interpreter fetching from ipfs.io is itself anomalous in most enterprises and the CID match is definitive. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/
ATT&CKT1105 T1102
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Web3/blockchain developer legitimately pinning or fetching content from ipfs.io via a Node app
  • CI jobs that pull assets from public IPFS gateways
  • Browser-based IPFS usage co-resident on a dev workstation (not node-initiated)
  • Analyst reproducing the fetch of the campaign CIDs in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("web3","blockchain") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "ipfs-http-client")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is node.exe and whether the URL contains a campaign CID (definitive) vs generic ipfs.io (assess node context). 2) Contain: isolate host, block ipfs.io egress for server/build subnets, kill the node process, and remove any sync.js written afterward. 3) Hunt: correlate the fetch time to a preceding @asyncapi install and a following connection to 85.137.53.71; check other hosts for the same CIDs and rotate credentials exposed to the environment.

    or (InitiatingProcessFileName has "node" and RemoteUrl contains "ipfs.io")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort

| order by conn_count desc

| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious @velora-dex/sdk (9.4.1/9.4.2) pulled into GitHub Actions build runner AIDelivery High
Hunts CI/build runners that install the trojanized @velora-dex/sdk npm package — the compromise that dropped a macOS backdoor the moment the SDK was imported. Version 9.4.0 is confirmed clean, so any install of a non-9.4.0 version of this specific package on a runner is suspect. Rationale: Anchors on the exact compromised package name '@velora-dex/sdk' and excludes the confirmed-clean 9.4.0, per Corgea (v9.4.1 published 2026-04-07) and StepSecurity — a named-package/version IOC that only fires on genuinely-affected installs. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence • https://github.com/VeloraDEX/sdk/issues/233
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer intentionally installing the clean 9.4.0 pin (excluded, but a lockfile resolving without an explicit version tag may show no version)
  • Internal mirror/registry proxy re-fetching the package name in log lines during cache warmup
  • Security researchers/DFIR reproducing the compromise in a sandbox runner
  • A vendored monorepo referencing 'velora-dex/sdk' in a path or comment picked up by broad command lines
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk@9.4.0") | where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the exact resolved version from the runner's package-lock.json/npm cache and the workflow run; 9.4.1/9.4.2 = confirmed malicious, 9.4.0 = clean. 2) Contain: isolate the runner (especially macOS/Bitrise hosts), revoke any secrets that were in scope for that job (Apple signing certs, App Store Connect keys, registry/deploy tokens), and rebuild the runner from a clean image. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'C2 beacon to Velora infra (89.36.224.5)' and the launchctl-persistence UC on the same DeviceId, and diff lockfiles across all repos for the pinned bad version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk"
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk@9.4.0" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk@9.4.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk"
| where not(ActingProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk@9.4.0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Build runner beacon/exfil to Velora backdoor C2 (89.36.224.5 / datahub.ink) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any outbound connection from a runner or endpoint to the confirmed Velora-SDK backdoor C2 infrastructure — IP 89.36.224.5 and domains datahub.ink, cloud-sync.online, byte-io.us. These are where the macOS implant fetched its shell script and exfiltrated harvested signing keys and tokens. Rationale: IP 89.36.224.5 is confirmed as the Velora backdoor C2 by StepSecurity, Corgea and Phoenix Security; the three domains are enumerated verbatim in Corgea's IOC list. Direct-hit IOC match, near-zero legitimate reason for a build host to reach these. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://phoenix.security/velora-dex-sdk-supply-chain-compromise-build-pipeline-injection-delivers-macos-persistent-implant/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox tooling actively probing the C2 (verify the initiating process is a scanner)
  • A newly-registered legitimate service reusing the 89.36.224.5 host after takedown (re-validate IP ownership)
  • Security team detonating the sample in an authorized lab connected to production telemetry
  • DNS sinkhole or passive-DNS collector resolving the domains for research
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("threatintel-scanner.exe","nessus","nmap")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the runner (node/npm/curl vs a legit tool) and the direction/volume of traffic to 89.36.224.5. 2) Contain: block the IP and three domains at egress/proxy, isolate the host, and immediately rotate every secret the affected build job could touch (Apple signing certs, provisioning profiles, App Store Connect keys, registry tokens). 3) Hunt: correlate against the @velora-dex/sdk install UC and the launchctl-persistence UC on the same host, and search all runners for prior connections to these indicators.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "89.36.224.5"
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("datahub.ink","cloud-sync.online","byte-io.us")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr == "89.36.224.5" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Indicator = DstIpAddr, Detail = Url),
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has_any ("datahub.ink","cloud-sync.online","byte-io.us") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Indicator = DnsQuery, Detail = DnsResponseName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Velora macOS backdoor launchctl persistence (com.apple.Terminal.profiler.plist) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the persistence artifacts the Velora SDK backdoor installs on macOS build runners: a masquerading LaunchAgent plist and support directory impersonating Apple's Terminal, plus the known payload hashes. Fires on the exact plist name, path, or file hash written to a runner. Rationale: com.apple.Terminal.profiler.plist and the ~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.Terminal/profiler directory are the exact persistence artifacts documented by Corgea; the plist name masquerades as Apple's Terminal but is not a genuine Apple file, so any write is high-fidelity. Payload SHA256s are the article-supplied IOCs, kept alongside the corroborated path artifacts. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://opensourcemalware.com/blog/velora-hacked • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Apple/Terminal update writing legitimately-named plists (the profiler variant is not a real Apple file, so overlap is unlikely)
  • EDR/DFIR tooling restoring a quarantined sample onto a lab host
  • Backup/restore software rehydrating a previously-infected user Library
  • Analyst manually copying the IOC file for reverse-engineering on a monitored host
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged macOS runner, confirm the plist exists under ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ and check `launchctl list` for the zsh.profiler service and the com.apple.Terminal/profiler support dir. 2) Contain: unload the LaunchAgent (launchctl bootout / remove plist), kill the profiler binary, isolate the host, and rotate all Apple signing material and CI secrets that lived on it. 3) Hunt: pivot to the 89.36.224.5 C2 UC and the @velora-dex/sdk install UC on the same DeviceId, and sweep the macOS fleet for the plist name and payload hashes.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" and FileName =~ "com.apple.Terminal.profiler.plist")
   or FolderPath has "com.apple.Terminal/profiler"
   or SHA256 in ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270","0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "com.apple.Terminal.profiler.plist" and TargetFilePath has "/LaunchAgents/")
   or TargetFilePath has "com.apple.Terminal/profiler"

npm/node install-time payload: package manager spawning curl/launchctl/osascript on a runner AIExploitation Medium
Behavioural catch for the Velora-class TTP where importing a poisoned npm package makes node call child_process.exec() to download and persist a payload. Surfaces node/npm/yarn/pnpm/bun spawning curl, wget, osascript, chmod or launchctl during a build — catching variants and future-versioned repackages the static IOCs miss. Rationale: Models the corroborated execution mechanism (dist/index.js calling child_process.exec() to curl a shell script then launchctl-persist) as a parent/child pivot, so it catches the campaign's behaviour beyond the pinned version/IOCs. Kept as hunting because legit postinstall scripts also spawn curl. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://phoenix.security/velora-dex-sdk-supply-chain-compromise-build-pipeline-injection-delivers-macos-persistent-implant/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate npm postinstall scripts (node-sass, node-gyp, puppeteer, esbuild) that curl/wget a prebuilt binary
  • Build scripts that chmod +x downloaded CLI tools
  • macOS packaging steps invoking osascript for notarization/UI prompts
  • Corporate proxy bootstrap scripts run under node during CI setup
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("registry.npmjs.org","github.com","githubusercontent.com","nodejs.org"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command line — a curl/wget to an unfamiliar host, a launchctl load of an unknown plist, or chmod +x on a freshly-downloaded file is malicious; a fetch to a known package CDN (github.com, npmjs.org) is likely benign. 2) Contain: if the destination or plist is unrecognised, isolate the runner and rotate its secrets. 3) Hunt: pivot on the downloaded host/IP against the C2 UC (89.36.224.5) and check for the launchctl-persistence plist on the same host; diff the repo lockfile for newly-added dependencies.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","yarn","pnpm","bun")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","osascript","launchctl","chmod")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","npm","yarn","pnpm","bun")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","osascript","launchctl","chmod")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud worm artifacts written on GitHub Actions runner (shai-hulud-workflow.yml / bundle.js) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the self-replicating Shai-Hulud npm worm's on-disk artifacts as they appear on a compromised runner: the shai-hulud-workflow.yml propagation workflow and the known malicious bundle.js payload hash. Distinct filesystem pivot from the Velora backdoor detections. Rationale: shai-hulud-workflow.yml is the worm's signature propagation artifact and 46faab8ab153...628f09 is the documented malicious bundle.js SHA-256, both corroborated by Unit42, Wiz and Datadog Security Labs — filesystem IOCs with no legitimate reason to exist on a runner. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher intentionally checking out an infected repo to a monitored host for analysis
  • IOC-sweep tooling writing sample copies of shai-hulud-workflow.yml to disk during hunting
  • A defensive canary/honeypot repo deliberately seeded with the artifact name
  • Backup restoration of a previously-infected repository working tree
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path/hash on the runner and identify the initiating process and the repo/workflow it landed in; a true hit means the worm executed and likely harvested tokens. 2) Contain: isolate the runner, revoke npm publish tokens and GitHub PATs the job held, and remove any pushed 'shai-hulud' branch / shai-hulud-workflow.yml from affected repos before it self-propagates. 3) Hunt: enumerate packages published by the compromised token, search for repos with the description marker 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming', and sweep all runners for the workflow filename and bundle.js hash.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "shai-hulud-workflow.yml"
   or SHA256 == "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "shai-hulud-workflow.yml"
   or TargetFileSHA256 =~ "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d") or SHA1 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d") or MD5 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d") or SHA1 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d") or MD5 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised @velora-dex/sdk npm package (9.4.1/9.4.2) installed on CI runner AIDelivery High
Hunts for the known-trojanized @velora-dex/sdk package landing in node_modules on a macOS/Windows/Linux build runner. Version 9.4.1 injected a base64 loader into dist/index.js that fires on import and pulls a macOS Go RAT (MiniRAT); 9.4.2 was the hurried revert — presence of either on a runner warrants review. Rationale: Anchors on the exact compromised package path '@velora-dex/sdk' confirmed by Corgea, safedep and StepSecurity; on an ephemeral CI runner any occurrence of this known-bad dependency is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://safedep.io/malicious-velora-dex-sdk-npm-compromised-rat/ • https://github.com/VeloraDEX/sdk/issues/233
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or internal IR team detonating the sample in a sandbox that is also EDR-monitored
  • A pinned lockfile deliberately holding 9.4.2 (reverted) for regression testing
  • Mirror/proxy cache warming that pre-fetches many package versions including these
  • A developer reproducing the advisory locally to confirm exposure
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cape.exe","procmon.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the repo/workflow that pulled @velora-dex/sdk and the exact version from the lockfile; check the runner's outbound connections to 89.36.224.5 in the same job window. 2) Contain: fail/cancel the pipeline, rotate every secret the job could touch (Apple signing certs, App Store Connect keys, Windows code-signing certs, OIDC/cloud tokens), and pin the dependency to a known-good pre-9.4.1 version or the vendor-verified fix. 3) Hunt: sweep all runners and developer macOS hosts for MiniRAT launchctl persistence and for egress to 89.36.224.5 / 216.126.225.129.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "@velora-dex/sdk" or FolderPath has @"@velora-dex\sdk"
| where FileName endswith ".js" or FileName =~ "package.json"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "@velora-dex/sdk" or TargetFilePath has "@velora-dex\\sdk"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CI runner egress to MiniRAT C2 89.36.224.5 (Velora SDK backdoor) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any outbound connection from a runner or build host to 89.36.224.5, the C2 that the injected @velora-dex/sdk loader contacts to fetch its architecture-specific macOS shell-script/Go RAT stager. A hard IOC — no legitimate build should reach this host. Rationale: 89.36.224.5 is the confirmed MiniRAT stager/C2 host (Corgea, safedep) referenced by the article's Velora SDK compromise; a single hard-IOC destination match needs no behavioural qualifier. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://safedep.io/malicious-velora-dex-sdk-npm-compromised-rat/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/scanning service that actively probes known C2 IPs from a monitored host
  • IR sandbox detonation of the sample with live network
  • Security team reproducing the advisory to validate blast radius
  • Shared NAT egress where a non-runner host on the same egress IP is the real source (verify DeviceName/src)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process (expect node/npm-spawned sh/curl) and whether @velora-dex/sdk is in the job's dependency tree. 2) Contain: block 89.36.224.5 at egress/firewall, isolate the runner/host, and rotate all secrets the pipeline exposed. 3) Hunt: pivot to launchctl persistence (MiniRAT) and to Megalodon C2 216.126.225.129:8443 across the fleet; review recent installs of @velora-dex/sdk org-wide.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "89.36.224.5"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "89.36.224.5"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CI runner egress to Megalodon secret-exfil C2 216.126.225.129:8443 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects outbound connections to 216.126.225.129 (notably TCP 8443), the confirmed Megalodon C2 that received compressed archives of harvested CI secrets, cloud creds, SSH keys and OIDC tokens via HTTPS POST across 5,500+ repos. Any runner reaching this host indicates active secret exfiltration. Rationale: 216.126.225.129:8443 is the corroborated Megalodon HTTPS-POST exfil C2 (StepSecurity, safedep, Phoenix); a destination-IP match is a hard IOC requiring no behavioural context. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/megalodon-mass-github-actions-secret-exfiltration-across-5-500-public-repositories • https://safedep.io/megalodon-mass-github-repo-backdooring-ci-workflows/ • https://phoenix.security/megalodon-ci-github-actions-workflow-poisoning-credential-harvesting/

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • IR sandbox detonation with live egress
  • Shared-egress NAT attributing another host's traffic to a runner (validate src/DeviceName)
  • Deliberate purple-team replay of the Megalodon workflow payload
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the runner/repo and confirm whether an injected workflow (e.g. SysDiag / Optimize-Build, forged authors build-bot/auto-ci/ci-bot/pipeline-bot) or malicious dependency initiated the connection; capture bytes sent. 2) Contain: block 216.126.225.129, cancel the pipeline, and treat every secret reachable by that job as compromised — rotate immediately. 3) Hunt: review GitHub Actions workflow files for base64 bash payloads POSTing to :8443, enumerate other repos with the same injected workflow, and correlate with @velora-dex/sdk installs and 89.36.224.5 egress.

| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession

| where DstIpAddr == "216.126.225.129"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

MiniRAT launchctl persistence established during macOS CI build AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for launchctl registering a LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon during a build, spawned from a shell/node/curl parent — the persistence step MiniRAT uses after the @velora-dex/sdk loader drops its arch-specific Go binary. Ephemeral GitHub-hosted macOS runners should never establish OS-level persistence mid-job. Rationale: Maps the MiniRAT launchctl-persistence step (StepSecurity/iru) to the parent chain (node-spawned shell → launchctl load) that a stager uses; on ephemeral runners any mid-build persistence is inherently anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence • https://www.iru.com/blog/minirat • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1543.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Xcode/fastlane or Homebrew setup steps that legitimately load helper LaunchAgents during app-signing jobs
  • Self-hosted macOS runner bootstrap scripts registering the runner service via launchctl
  • Rosetta/simulator tooling loading daemons on first run
  • Developer macOS host installing a legitimate background service via a shell installer
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "actions.runner" and ProcessCommandLine !has "com.github.actions" and ProcessCommandLine !has "fastlane"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the launchctl target plist path and the referenced program binary; confirm the grandparent traces to node/npm and whether @velora-dex/sdk is present or 89.36.224.5 was contacted. 2) Contain: kill the persistence item (launchctl bootout / unload), quarantine the dropped binary, isolate the host, and rotate signing certs/keys handled by that runner. 3) Hunt: search DeviceFileEvents for plist writes to ~/Library/LaunchAgents or /Library/LaunchDaemons during builds and pivot to the two campaign C2 IPs across all macOS hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "launchctl"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("load","bootstrap","submit")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","node","curl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "launchctl"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("load","bootstrap","submit")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","zsh","node","curl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm/node lifecycle script fetching Bun runtime from github.com/oven-sh/bun AIInstallation High
Detects an npm preinstall/postinstall lifecycle script (node.exe parented by npm) reaching out to github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases to download the Bun v1.3.13 runtime. This is the exact bootstrap behaviour of the TeamPCP @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 payload (bw_setup.js Stage-1) and is highly anomalous on developer endpoints because legitimate JS projects rarely pull Bun via a package-install hook. Rationale: Article explicitly names github.com/oven-sh/bun and Bun v1.3.13 as the runtime downloaded by Stage-1 bw_setup.js during npm preinstall — pairing the github.com/oven-sh/bun URL token with an npm-family parent process is a near-zero-FP signature on production endpoints (developer laptops will produce occasional FPs, hence the parent-process pinning). Cross-checked against Socket and Checkmarx advisories listed below. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/teampcp-bitwarden-cli-supply-chain • https://checkmarx.com/blog/checkmarx-supply-chain-incident-april-2026/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer intentionally installing Bun via an npm/yarn install script on a workstation
  • CI/CD build agent (GitHub Actions/Jenkins) running 'curl ... github.com/oven-sh/bun/install.sh | bash' in a job
  • Internal devtool wrapper that bootstraps a Bun toolchain on first run
  • Open-source project benchmark suites that download Bun in their install step
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "jenkins" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "runner\\_work" and DeviceName !startswith "build-" and DeviceName !startswith "ci-" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\actions-runner\\"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull the full process tree (npm/node parent → downloader child → Bun URL) and the downloaded artifact's SHA256. Check whether the package the user just installed is on the published TeamPCP IOC list (@bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 and any sibling Checkmarx packages). Inspect npm cache (~/.npm/_cacache and %AppData%\npm-cache) for the offending package and its preinstall script. Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host, rotate every credential reachable from it (npm tokens, GitHub PATs, cloud CLI creds, SSH keys, .env secrets, Docker/kubeconfig), revoke any GitHub PAT touched in the last 30 days, and block egress to audit.checkmarx[.]cx + 94.154.172[.]43 at the perimeter. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot on the user's npm/GitHub identity for new public repos containing the string 'Shai-Hulud: The Third Coming', then sweep the org for any other host that downloaded github.com/oven-sh/bun via an npm parent in the last 30 days.
let bunUrlIndicators = dynamic(["github.com/oven-sh/bun", "oven-sh/bun/releases", "bun-windows-x64", "bun-linux-x64", "bun-darwin"]);
let npmParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","npm-cli.js","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe"]);
let downloaderChildren = dynamic(["node.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","wget.exe","bun.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","pwsh.exe"]);
// Process-tree pivot — npm parent spawning a downloader child with Bun URL on the command line
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (npmParents) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (npmParents)
    | where FileName in~ (downloaderChildren)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (bunUrlIndicators) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (bunUrlIndicators)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
              ParentImage = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
              InitImage  = InitiatingProcessFileName,
              InitCmd    = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              ChildImage = FileName,
              ChildCmd   = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
// Network pivot — same process families connecting to github.com for the Bun release tarball
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where RemoteUrl has "github.com" and (RemoteUrl has "oven-sh/bun" or RemoteUrl has "bun-windows" or RemoteUrl has "bun-linux" or RemoteUrl has "bun-darwin")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (downloaderChildren)
    | where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (npmParents) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (npmParents)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName,
              AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              ParentImage = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
              InitImage   = InitiatingProcessFileName,
              InitCmd     = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              ChildImage  = "<network-egress>", ChildCmd = RemoteUrl, SHA256 = InitiatingProcessSHA256;
union ProcHits, NetHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let bunUrlIndicators = dynamic(["github.com/oven-sh/bun", "oven-sh/bun/releases", "bun-windows-x64", "bun-linux-x64", "bun-darwin"]);
let npmParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","npm-cli.js","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe","npm","node","yarn","pnpm","npx"]);
let downloaderChildren = dynamic(["node.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","wget.exe","bun.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","pwsh.exe","node","curl","wget","bun","bash","sh","pwsh"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any (downloaderChildren) or ParentProcessName has_any (downloaderChildren)
| where (ParentProcessName has_any (npmParents) or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (npmParents) or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (npmParents))
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (bunUrlIndicators) or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (bunUrlIndicators)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects an npm/yarn/pnpm install lifecycle script (Node.js parented by npm) spawning a downloader to fetch the Bun JavaScript runtime from github.com/oven-sh/bun — the Stage-1 bootstrap of the TeamPCP @bitwarden/cli supply-chain payload.

  selection_child:

level: high

C2 beacon to audit.checkmarx[.]cx /v1/telemetry (TeamPCP Shai-Hulud Third Coming) AICommand & Control High
Detects any outbound network/DNS activity to the TeamPCP C2 audit.checkmarx[.]cx (94.154.172.43) — particularly POSTs to the /v1/telemetry path — that exfiltrates harvested cloud, CI/CD and developer credentials from compromised hosts. The domain visually impersonates Checkmarx's legitimate infrastructure but resolves to attacker-controlled space. Rationale: Article Table 1 names the C2 server, IP and HTTP path explicitly (audit.checkmarx[.]cx:443 / 94.154.172.43 / /v1/telemetry) — any hit on these three indicators is a confirmed-compromise signal, not a hunting hypothesis. Corroborated by Checkmarx's official disclosure that all four artifact families (npm, Docker Hub, GitHub Actions, VS Code) shared this C2. Cross-checked against: • https://checkmarx.com/blog/checkmarx-supply-chain-incident-april-2026/ • https://socket.dev/blog/teampcp-bitwarden-cli-supply-chain

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst manually visiting the domain during IR triage (filter on known analyst workstation/jump-host)
  • Threat-intel sandbox or scanner deliberately resolving the IOC (e.g. a TI enrichment service hosted on the corporate network)
  • Outbound proxy/DLP solution generating a synthetic resolution for the indicator feed
  • Endpoint EDR sensor itself pulling the indicator for local matching (filter on MsSense.exe / SenseIR.exe)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and DeviceName !in~ ("soc-jump-01","ir-analyst-vm")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull every host that resolved audit.checkmarx[.]cx or connected to 94.154.172.43 in the last 30 days; for each, identify the initiating process and user. Capture the full HTTPS request body if proxy decryption is available — POST to /v1/telemetry carries exfiltrated tokens. Step 2 — Contain: Block audit.checkmarx[.]cx and 94.154.172.43 at DNS, proxy and firewall. Force-rotate every npm token, GitHub PAT, AWS/GCP/Azure CLI credential, Docker Hub token and .env-stored secret on every connecting host within the last 24h. Step 3 — Hunt: For each affected user, list every npm package and GitHub repo they own — TeamPCP's worm republishes packages and creates public 'Shai-Hulud: The Third Coming' repos under the victim identity. Pivot to UC #3 (file artifacts) and UC #1 (Bun download).
let c2Hosts = dynamic(["audit.checkmarx.cx", "audit.checkmarx[.]cx"]);
let c2Ips    = dynamic(["94.154.172.43"]);
let c2Path   = "/v1/telemetry";
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteUrl has_any (c2Hosts)) or (RemoteIP in (c2Ips)) or (RemoteUrl has c2Path and RemotePort in (443, 80))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2Hosts = dynamic(["audit.checkmarx.cx"]);
let c2Ips    = dynamic(["94.154.172.43"]);
let c2Path   = "/v1/telemetry";
union isfuzzy=true
(
  ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstHostname has_any (c2Hosts) or DstIpAddr in (c2Ips) or (isnotempty(Url) and Url has c2Path and DstPortNumber in (443, 80))
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
),
(
  ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has_any (c2Hosts)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsQueryTypeName, DnsResponseCodeName
),
(
  ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where HttpHostName has_any (c2Hosts) or Url has c2Path and (HttpHostName has "checkmarx.cx")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode
),
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationHostName has_any (c2Hosts) or DestinationIP in (c2Ips) or RequestURL has "audit.checkmarx.cx" or RequestURL has c2Path
  | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TeamPCP Shai-Hulud C2 audit.checkmarx[.]cx Connection
id: 7e5a3b2c-1f4d-4a6e-9b8f-3c2d1e4f5a62
status: experimental
description: Detects connections or DNS resolutions to the TeamPCP / Shai-Hulud Third Coming C2 infrastructure (audit.checkmarx[.]cx / 94.154.172.43) used by the @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 npm supply-chain payload and the broader Checkmarx-distribution-channel compromise to exfiltrate harvested credentials via /v1/telemetry.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/monitoring-npm-supply-chain-attacks/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/20
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1041
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_domain:
    QueryName|contains:
      - 'audit.checkmarx.cx'
  selection_ip:
    QueryResults|contains:
      - '94.154.172.43'
  condition: selection_domain or selection_ip
falsepositives:
  - None expected; the domain is attacker-controlled and not Checkmarx's real infrastructure (legitimate Checkmarx uses checkmarx.com / checkmarx.net).
level: critical
(@network.destination.domain:audit.checkmarx.cx OR CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 94.154.172.43/32) OR @http.url:*audit.checkmarx.cx* OR @http.url:*/v1/telemetry* OR @dns.question.name:*audit.checkmarx.cx*)
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/audit\.checkmarx\.cx/i)
OR (#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="94.154.172.43")
OR (#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP6 (RemoteAddressIP6=*94.154.172.43* OR ContextImageFileName=/(node|bun|npm)/i AND RemotePort=443))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
(`cim_Network_Traffic_indexes` (dest="audit.checkmarx.cx" OR dest="audit.checkmarx[.]cx" OR dest_ip="94.154.172.43")) OR (`cim_Network_Resolution_indexes` query="*audit.checkmarx.cx*") OR (`cim_Web_indexes` (url="*audit.checkmarx.cx*" OR dest="audit.checkmarx.cx") (url="*/v1/telemetry*" OR uri_path="/v1/telemetry")) | stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime count by host src dest dest_ip url http_method app | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Malicious @bitwarden/cli payload artifacts on disk (bw_setup.js, bw1.js, Shai-Hulud markers) AIInstallation High
Detects creation or execution of the Stage-1 (bw_setup.js) and Stage-2 (bw1.js) Node.js scripts dropped by the TeamPCP @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 npm package, as well as the 'Shai-Hulud: The Third Coming' string written into public repo content that the worm uses as an attribution marker and propagation beacon. This catches both the install-time drop on the npm install path and any post-compromise replay. Rationale: Article explicitly names bw_setup.js (Stage-1 bootstrap, registered as the `bw` bin) and bw1.js (Stage-2 Bun payload) inside the malicious @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 package. The legitimate Bitwarden CLI ships neither filename, so the filename + package path combo is a hard-IOC match. The Shai-Hulud Third Coming string is a TeamPCP attribution marker per the article body. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/teampcp-bitwarden-cli-supply-chain • https://github.com/bitwarden/clients/security/advisories
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546.016 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher unzipping a captured copy of the malicious package on an analyst workstation for analysis (filter on known analyst hosts)
  • Threat-intel ingestion pipeline downloading the package from npm cache for IOC extraction
  • SOC sandbox/detonation environment replaying the package install
  • Legitimate package named 'bw1.js' or 'bw_setup.js' shipped by an unrelated internal project (unlikely; verify against package.json)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\sandboxes\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\detonation\\" and DeviceName !startswith "ti-sandbox-" and DeviceName !startswith "malware-analysis-"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Capture the dropping process tree and the surrounding package.json — confirm version is 2026.4.0 and that the preinstall script invokes bw_setup.js. Hash bw1.js and submit to threat intel. Step 2 — Contain: Isolate host, run `npm uninstall -g @bitwarden/cli` and `npm cache clean --force`, wipe ~/.npm/_cacache, kill any lingering bun.exe / node.exe processes parented by npm, rotate all credentials reachable from the host (npm token, GitHub PAT, cloud CLI tokens, .env secrets, SSH keys). Step 3 — Hunt: Query the user's GitHub for any new public repository created in the last 30 days containing the string 'Shai-Hulud: The Third Coming' — this is the worm's propagation marker — and audit every npm package the user can publish for unauthorised releases.
let stageFiles = dynamic(["bw_setup.js", "bw1.js"]);
let packageHints = dynamic(["@bitwarden\\cli", "@bitwarden/cli", "node_modules\\@bitwarden\\cli", "node_modules/@bitwarden/cli"]);
let shaiHuludMarker = "Shai-Hulud: The Third Coming";
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where (FileName in~ (stageFiles)) or (FolderPath has_any (packageHints) and FileName endswith ".js") or (AdditionalFields has shaiHuludMarker)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName,
              AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
              FolderPath, FileName, SHA256;
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npm-cli.js","bun.exe")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (stageFiles)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
              FolderPath, FileName = FileName, SHA256, ProcCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
union FileHits, ProcHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let stageFiles = dynamic(["bw_setup.js", "bw1.js"]);
let packageHints = dynamic(["@bitwarden\\cli", "@bitwarden/cli", "node_modules\\@bitwarden\\cli", "node_modules/@bitwarden/cli"]);
let npmRunners = dynamic(["npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npm-cli.js","bun.exe","npm","node","yarn","pnpm","bun"]);
let FileHits = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where (TargetFileName in~ (stageFiles)) or (TargetFilePath has_any (packageHints) and TargetFileExtension =~ "js")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
              ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
              TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256;
let ProcHits = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any (npmRunners) or ParentProcessName has_any (npmRunners)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (stageFiles)
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
              ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
              ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
              TargetFilePath = "", TargetFileName = "", TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256;
union FileHits, ProcHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Unauthenticated access to MantisBT admin/install.php on a production host (CVE-2026-52847) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts for HTTP requests that reach /admin/install.php with a 200 response after deployment. The installer should be removed/restricted post-install; its continued reachability is both the precondition for the reflected-XSS chain and a recon signal. Rationale: Uses the exact installer path /admin/install.php named in the advisory plus a 200-status filter; the installer's reachability is the stated precondition for the whole XSS chain and the workaround is to remove /admin. Corroborated against the GitLab advisory DB entry for CVE-2026-52847. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-52847/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-52881/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vcrw-4xvv-jh49
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin performing an in-place upgrade or fresh install of MantisBT
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) probing the endpoint
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring configured to hit the app root that redirects into the installer
  • DevOps CI pipeline validating a freshly deployed MantisBT container
  • Security team running an authorized pentest against the tracker
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8") and csUserAgent !has "Nessus" and csUserAgent !has "Qualys"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the source IP is not an authorized admin/scanner and whether the MantisBT version is <=2.28.3. Review the csUriQuery values returned for injected HTML tokens (form/meta). Step 2 (contain): Remove or ACL-restrict the /admin directory per the vendor workaround, or upgrade to 2.28.4+; block external access to /admin/install.php at the WAF/reverse proxy. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same source IP across web logs for other admin-path probing and for follow-on requests carrying reflected-XSS payloads (see the form-injection and meta-redirect UCs).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem endswith "/admin/install.php"
| where scStatus == 200
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Queries = make_set(csUriQuery, 20) by cIP, csUriStem, csMethod, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by Hits desc

Credential-phishing form injection via reflected XSS in MantisBT install.php (CVE-2026-52881) AIDelivery High
Detects HTTP requests to /admin/install.php whose query string carries injected <form>/action markup — the credential-phishing primitive the advisory calls out, enabled by the missing CSP form-action directive. The payload is reflected from user-supplied parameters via print_test_result(). Rationale: Targets the advisory's explicit 'credential-phishing form injection' primitive using the concrete injector path /admin/install.php and injected <form action=...> tokens (both raw and URL-encoded). The missing form-action CSP directive means the injected form is the actual exploitation vector, making these tokens high-fidelity. Confirmed via GitLab CVE-2026-52881 advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/mantisbt/mantisbt/CVE-2026-52881/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vcrw-4xvv-jh49
ATT&CKT1598.003 T1189 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentester/bug-bounty tester replaying the watchTowr PoC against the tracker
  • A generic web vulnerability scanner (Burp/ZAP/Nuclei) firing XSS templates that include <form> payloads
  • A legitimate query parameter that coincidentally contains the literal string 'action=http' (e.g. a callback/return URL param)
  • WAF audit-mode traffic replaying attack corpora
Suppression filter
| where csUriQuery has_any ("<form", "%3Cform", "formaction") // require an actual form tag, not just action=http return-URL params
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Decode the csUriQuery and confirm an injected <form> with an action pointing off-host; note the target action domain as attacker credential-harvest infra. Step 2 (contain): Block the source IP and the harvest domain at the WAF/proxy, and restrict/remove /admin/install.php or upgrade to MantisBT 2.28.4+. Step 3 (hunt): Search web logs for any admin sessions or credential POSTs to the identified harvest domain, and pivot on the source IP for the meta-redirect variant and installer-probe activity.

| where csUriStem endswith "/admin/install.php"
| where csUriQuery has_any ("<form", "%3Cform", "formaction", "form%20action", "action=http", "action%3Dhttp", "method=post", "method%3Dpost")
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csMethod, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
